title: The sage
hookLine: the sage has no house to guard and no friendships built on fear

lines: A WORD FOR SOMEONE WITHOUT THEM.
cards: Count the things you have to keep an eye on. Passwords. The car's next service.
The plant that's dying. Subscriptions you forgot. Friends who'd be upset if you didn't reply by tonight.
None of it is bad. But each one is a small hook, and some days a life is mostly hooks. The Buddha's India had a word for a person who'd taken most of the hooks out.
Not a priest, not a scholar. Someone quiet, wise, unattached, often wandering. The twelfth poem of the Sutta Nipata is about that person.

teach.b: Muni means sage, a silent, wise one. The Buddha himself is called Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakya people. The Muni Sutta opens with a strong line.
From intimacy, fear is born. From a home, dust arises. To be without a home and without that kind of clinging: that's the sage's way of seeing.
It sounds harsh until you hear the word underneath. Santhava, the intimacy here, means acquaintance, familiarity, and the commentary reads it as the binding kind, closeness held by craving.
Closeness like that comes with fear of losing it. The sage isn't cold; it's the clinging the poem warns against. Then come pictures.

teach.h: A POST AT THE BATHING PLACE
teach.b: The sage stands firm, like a post at a river's bathing place, while other people talk in extremes around it, praise and blame splashing on every side.
The sage lives on what is given, and doesn't flatter the giver or complain about the gift.

At the very end comes a frank image: a blue-necked peacock never matches the speed of a swan in flight, and in the same way, the poem says, a householder doesn't match a sage meditating alone in the forest.

That's the poem's view of the wandering life. Other Buddhist texts honor lay life and remember lay followers who were wise teachers. One more twist, from the Dhammapada: nobody becomes a muni just by keeping silent.
A fool can be quiet. The sage is the one who weighs things well and chooses the good.

how: Buddhists call the Buddha Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas, and the ideal of the quiet, unattached sage runs through the poems of the Sutta Nipata.

o: a monk under a vow never to speak
a priest who performs the fire rites
a sage, a silent and wise one

games.q: the sage poem: tap the pairs.
p: a sage, a silent wise one
the sage of the Sakya people
the sage amid praise and blame
a post at the bathing place

s: the Buddha is often called Sakyamuni
the sage of the Sakya people, his clan.
anyone who keeps silent is a muni
the Dhammapada says silence alone doesn't make a sage; weighing well and choosing the good does.
the Muni Sutta says the sage should have no friends at all
it warns against closeness that breeds fear, the friendships built on clinging.

games.q: you're at a crowded river where people are shouting praise and blame at one another. how does the poem picture the sage?
o: standing firm, like a post at the bathing place.
games.why: the sage stays steady like a post at a bathing place while others talk in extremes all around.

practice: Notice one tie in your life that runs on fear, a reply you dread being late with, an approval you keep checking for, and without cutting anyone off, breathe out and let the fear loosen.
Then picture the post at the river, praise and blame splashing around it, and feel yourself that steady for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Muni. A sage, a silent wise one: no house to guard, no friendships built on fear, steady as a post while praise and blame splash by. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit muni: sage. in the Buddha's title Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas.

carryVoice: Your line: stand like the post. Praise and blame splash by; the post stays. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 268–269 (not by silence alone is one a muni)
